answer_plain: Giving the same total water in one go and then every ten days changes hydrogen uptake over two weeks by about -5.5 % relative to a single rain, but it may go up or down (from 48 % lower to 175 % higher). Spreading it every three days gives about 37 % less (68 % less to 129 % more) and daily drip about 38 % less (73 % less to 136 % more). One possible reason is that frequent small doses mostly evaporate from the surface.
answer_science: Delivering the same irrigation volume, on top of the 12 mm rain, daily, every three days or every ten days changed 14-day H₂ uptake by a median of −29 %, −27 % and +2.5 %, respectively. The 90 % intervals of all three schedules include both decreases and increases (−73 to +136 %, −68 to +129 % and −48 to +175 %). Irrigation acts in two directions in the twin: it lengthens the period above the activation threshold, and it fills pores, which slows H₂ diffusion to the reacting community. The balance is set by the retention curve; the air-entry potential ψ_e and the retention exponent b explain most of the variance for the ten-day schedule (S_T = 0.61 and 0.40). Ranking the schedules therefore requires a measured retention curve for Rub' al Khali sand.
baseline_label: One 12 mm rain on day 1, no irrigation

limits_plain: The range shows how much the answer moves when uncertain numbers in the models are varied; the models themselves could also be wrong. Pipe layout, root uptake and uneven wetting around drip emitters are not represented.
limits_science: The irrigation volume follows the FAO-56 order-of-magnitude crop demand and is a scenario input. The twin uses one well-mixed 10 cm layer, so drip emitters, wetting fronts and deeper drainage are represented only through the daily water balance of that layer.
